intro.heading: The last audit was in spring. It is now October.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A registered manager knows the service looks clean. Cleaning schedules run, hand gel is topped up and staff did their annual refresher in the summer. The last audit was done in spring, on paper, and it scored well. Now the evenings are drawing in and she wants a fresh look before the colder months. The trouble is that a folder of old forms cannot tell her what has changed since, which checks were missed, or who was meant to fix what.

trail.text: The last audit is done and filed. The score is good.
Cleaning schedules run, hand gel is topped up and the annual refresher is completed.
The manager decides to repeat the audit in autumn, ahead of the colder months.
The spring audit is still in a folder. Nobody has looked at it since.
A hand gel dispenser was not refitted on one corridor. Nobody told the manager.
Two sluice and laundry checks were skipped. No photo, no owner, no date.
The weather turns, and the paper audit is still the latest evidence you have.
An inspector asks when you last audited infection control and what you changed.

trail_close: Doing the audit was not the hard part. The hard part is finding the gaps early, giving each one an owner and showing that it was fixed.

why.heading: Why autumn is the time to audit
why.sub: A winter audit finds problems you then have to live with. An autumn audit finds them while you can still act.

cards.title: Time to fix what you find
cards.body: An audit in October leaves weeks to replace a dispenser, retrain a shift or re-order stock. One run in the middle of a busy spell only tells you what has already gone wrong.

cards.title: Paper hides the pattern
cards.body: A pile of old forms rarely shows whether the same question keeps failing. A saved score for each section shows where the weak spots are, and whether they are moving.

cards.title: A score without actions is a number
cards.body: Finding a gap helps nobody until someone owns it. Every gap needs a named person, a date and proof that it was done, so the next audit can check it.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: Why audit in autumn and not wait for the next quarter?
items.a: Because you get time to act. An audit in October finds the empty dispenser, the skipped check or the out of date schedule while there are still weeks to put it right. You can keep your normal schedule as well. This is simply a deliberate check before the colder months.

It depends on the service. The Infection Control Audit is monthly and checks practice, cleaning, equipment and outbreak readiness. Infection Control is quarterly and covers general precautions, specimen handling, waste, laundry, pest control, staff health, food safety and MRSA management. For care at home there is the Home Care Infection Prevention and PPE Audit, run once a month for each care worker.

Yes. Audits are free on every plan, including the Free plan. You get the library, scoring, photos, the PDF report, actions, scheduling and approval. Recommendations from our own machine learning and the drafted action plan are on the paid plans only. You can create a free account to look around.

items.q: Do my staff need to sit at a computer to do it?
items.a: No. Audits run in the Staff Hub, a web app that works on a phone, tablet or desktop. The auditor walks the corridor, answers each question and adds a photo where it helps. Staff only see the audits you allocate to them.

items.q: What does the score tell me?
items.a: It is the share of scored questions that passed, shown for the whole audit and for each section. That points you to the weak section. It is CareStream's own score. It is not a CQC rating, and an audit is not a record that you send to the regulator.

items.q: What happens to the things we find?
items.a: Each gap becomes an action with an owner and a due date. The owner sees it in the hub, can ask for more time and can add photo proof when it is done. At the next audit of the same kind, the earlier actions are listed and the auditor marks each one fixed or not fixed.

items.q: Can I link a weak result to training?
items.a: You can link any audit to the free infection prevention and control course or to your own training modules, so the finished audit offers them. A manager still decides who needs what, and nothing is sent automatically. You can also set up short adhoc training on the paid plans.
Create a free account, open the audit library and schedule your first audit. The paid plans have a 14 day free trial if you want the extra features. See the pricing page for what each plan includes.

limits.heading: What CareStream does not do here

cards.title: It does not replace walking the building
cards.body: An audit records what a person sees and answers. Someone still has to look at the dispenser, open the sluice door and watch a colleague wash their hands.

cards.title: The score is not a CQC rating
cards.body: Audit scores are CareStream's own, and an audit is not a record submitted to the regulator. Use it to find and fix gaps and to show what you did about them.

cards.title: It cannot give you an outbreak plan
cards.body: The audits ask whether your arrangements are in place. They do not write your outbreak plan or give clinical advice. Follow the guidance for your service and your local health protection team.

items.q: What is an infection prevention audit?
items.a: It is a structured check of how well your service prevents and controls infection, covering practice, cleaning, equipment, waste and laundry. A scored, repeatable audit lets you compare one round with the next. Read more in our guide to auditing infection control.

items.q: How often should we audit infection control?
items.a: That is for you to decide from your own risk assessment. In CareStream the Infection Control Audit starts as monthly and Infection Control as quarterly, and you can set a repeat when you schedule it. The Hand Hygiene Observation Audit is monthly too.

items.q: Is there an infection control audit tool I can use free?
items.a: CareStream's audit library is free on every plan, including the Free plan. It includes scoring, photos, a PDF report, actions and scheduling. Other free tools exist, so choose the one your team will actually use. See the audit library.

items.q: Do you have an audit checklist for care at home?
items.a: Yes. The Home Care Infection Prevention and PPE Audit has 44 questions, run monthly for each care worker. It covers PPE use, hand hygiene, waste, laundry, spillages, uniform and training.

items.q: Can staff do the audit on their own phone?
items.a: Yes, if you give them Staff + Audits access and tick the audits they can run. They use the Staff Hub in a browser or as an installed app. Admins can run every audit.

items.q: Do I get a report I can show someone?
items.a: Yes. A finished audit gives you a PDF report. It can also go through a manager sign off first if you switch that on in Settings. Remember that the score is CareStream's own, not a CQC rating.

items.q: How do I prove that a gap was fixed?
items.a: The action owner marks it done, adds a note and can attach up to 10 photos. At the next audit of the same kind the auditor checks the earlier actions, and a gap that is not fixed reopens.

items.q: Where do the rules come from?
items.a: The Regulated Activities Regulations 2014, regulation 12 sets out safe care and treatment, including preventing and controlling infection. A government code of practice on preventing and controlling infections also applies to adult social care providers in England. Your audit helps show you are acting on both.

guide.heading: A practical autumn audit of infection control
guide.lede: You do not need a big project. You need a date, a person, a good audit checklist and a way to keep the results together.

sections.h3: Set it up so it actually happens
paragraphs: Pick one audit and book it in with a named person and a date, rather than leaving it as an intention. If you already audit every month or quarter, treat this round as the one you finish before the colder months. Decide in advance which areas will be walked, so the check does not drift towards the easy ones.
Under regulation 12, providers must assess the risk of, and prevent, detect and control the spread of, infections. A repeatable audit gives you a dated record of how you did that in your own service.

sections.h3: Four steps for the week of the audit
checklist: Schedule the infection prevention audit with a named person and a due date.
Walk the areas with a phone, answer every question and add a photo for each gap.
Turn every gap into an action with an owner, a date and a priority.
Add the next date to your calendar, so last time's actions are checked at the next audit.

sections.h3: Make the follow up the habit
paragraphs: The audit finds, but the actions fix. Review open actions in your regular management meeting, ask owners for proof and let the next audit confirm the fix. Where a weak section points to a skills gap, link the audit to the infection prevention and control course so the training is one tap away.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep each audit, its photos, the actions with owners and the re-check together, so you can show what you found, what you changed and when.
